title: e2e-latency-profiling-summary-2026-03-04
content:
Summary:

This note summarizes the end-to-end latency traces we collected for the serving runtime during the March 3-4 sampling window. Focus is on p50/p95/p99 and per-stage breakdowns for the rw-13b and rw-70b model variants under typical production traffic and a small synthetic probe. The goal: identify dominant tail contributors and propose targeted mitigations for p95/p99.

Top-line numbers (production sampled, 99th percentile sampling weight):
- rw-13b (quantized int8, 8k context) – p50: 140 ms, p95: 420 ms, p99: 950 ms
- rw-70b (float16, 8k context) – p50: 380 ms, p95: 1,200 ms, p99: 2,600 ms
- Hosted small model (rw-3b, int8) – p50: 95 ms, p95: 260 ms, p99: 560 ms

Methodology:
- Trace collection: production-sampled traces (1 in 200 requests) + controlled synthetic probes (bursty and steady) over 24h.
- Tracing coverage: ingress -> auth -> routing -> tokenization -> model forward (kernel exec) -> kv-cache lookup -> decoding/token generation -> post-processing -> response serialization -> egress.
- Each trace contains per-stage start/end timestamps and selected kernel/hardware metadata where available.
- Traces were aggregated and bucketed by model, route, and request size (short prompt <128 tokens, long prompt 1024+).

Representative per-stage breakdown (rw-13b, p99 = 950 ms):
- Ingress (load-balancer + TLS handshake): 30 ms (3%)
- Auth/quotas: 12 ms (1%)
- Routing + queue wait (prioritization): 110 ms (12%) — highly variance-sensitive on burst events
- Tokenization: 8 ms (1%)
- KV-cache lookup (cold): 75 ms (8%) — cold misses dominate tails when prefix caching not present
- Model forward (compute + kernel enqueue): 490 ms (52%) — large contributor to median and tail (GPU scheduling jitter + cross-stream interference)
- Decoding (sampling + logits->token): 140 ms (15%) — decoder kernel stalls on blocked prefetch and small-batch inefficiencies
- Post-processing (safety checks, formatting): 15 ms (1%)
- Response serialization + egress: 70 ms (7%)

Notes on variability sources:
- Queue wait/routing: During short bursts we see priority inversion where long-running requests preempt the fast-path, causing p95 spikes. Observed correlation between route-level concurrency and routing queue wait.
- KV-cache cold misses: p99 traces frequently include cold KV lookups caused by tenant-specific prefixes or new completeness of prompt prefixes. Cold misses also amplify model forward times (more tokens to compute).
- GPU scheduling jitter: model forward p99 is often attributable to cross-workload contention on the same GPU, sometimes due to background maintenance jobs and occasional fallback to a less-optimized kernel path for longer sequences.
- Decoder stalls: small-batch decoding is not fully amortized; the decoder kernel launches are serialized when multiple small requests hit the same stream.

Comparison: production sampled vs synthetic probe:
- Synthetic steady load (controlled, pinned capacity) shows tighter tails: rw-13b p99 ~ 720 ms. Production p99 is worse due to background interference and cold cache effect.

Immediate actionable items (short-term, low-effort):
1) Increase prefix caching TTL and warm-up for high-traffic tenants — target reduction in KV-cache cold misses for p95/p99. Owner: Lina Gomez.
2) Route-level concurrency cap for known latency-sensitive routes (soft cap + fast-path reservation). Quick experiments: reserve 10% of capacity for fast-path. Owner: Daniel Kim.
3) Prioritize small-batch decoder consolidation: implement opportunistic batching for decoders when stream-friendly. Owner: Marcus Lee.
4) Add trace-level tagging for kernel selection path to measure frequency of fallback kernels. Owner: Aisha Patel.

Medium-term (engineering work):
- Implement preemption-aware scheduler on GPU host to reduce cross-stream interference; explore migrating low-priority background jobs to isolated hosts.
- Kernel autotuner: record sequence-length distribution and select optimized kernels preemptively during warm start.
- Smart KV prefetch for common prefixes detected across a customer tenant.

Metrics we should track post-change:
- p95 and p99 per-route and per-tenant (daily)
- Fraction of traces with queue wait > 100 ms
- KV-cache miss rate at p95/p99
- Frequency of fallback kernel usage and associated delta in model forward time

Outstanding questions / follow-ups:
- Can we correlate specific tenant rollout events with p99 spikes? (e.g., new model versions, sudden traffic pattern changes)
- Are there any maintenance jobs that run on a rolling schedule that line up with increased p99? Need SRE calendar cross-check.
- Evaluate cost/benefit of reserving a small GPU pool for latency-sensitive routes vs. software-only mitigations.

Appendix — sample traces and examples (excerpt):
- Trace A (rw-13b, p99): ingress 28 ms | routing queue 180 ms | kv-cache cold 82 ms | forward 520 ms | decode 120 ms | egress 20 ms -> total 950 ms.
- Trace B (rw-70b, p99): forward 2,100 ms dominated by kernel fallback during long seq -> total 2,600 ms.

Next steps:
- Triage owners to pick the short-term items and start an experiment plan. I propose a 2-week sprint to validate 1) TTL/warmer changes and 2) route-level reservation. Measure delta on p95/p99 for top 10 latency-sensitive routes.

Notes to self / loose items:
- Add GC/sidecar pause telemetry if we can to rule out host-level pauses.
- Cross-link to perf-tests PR with controlled preemption simulation once ready.

End of note.
